item.title: Renal handling of urea
item.description:
contributes 50% of osmolality in renal medulla this drives water reabsorption at glomerulus: freely filtered proximal tubule: 50% reabsorbed passively secreted into ascending limb down concentration gradient from medullary interstitium = tubular concentration of urea ↑ distal collecting duct, cortical collecting duct: impermeable to urea as water gets reabsorbed, concentration of urea ↑ inner medullary collecting ducts: passively reabsorbed via urea transporters → medullary interstitium
ADH increases activation of epithelial uniporters → facilitated diffusion of urea out of collecting duct
#renal

item.title: Endothelial function
item.description:
Responsible for Autoregulation via sensing shear stressresponsible for increased permeability in septic shock not its fault tbhcopied from Deranged Physiology Forms the interface between the vessel wall and moving blood. Acts as the exclusion zone between blood cells and the endothelium Acts as a barrier against leakage of fluid, proteins and lipids across the vascular wall. Interacts dynamically with blood constituents. Acts the "molecular sieve" for plasma proteins, forming the basis of the Starling principle and acting as the origin of the oncotic forces which control the transcapillary movement of water. → THIS is the semi-permeable membrane Modulates adhesion of inflammatory cells and platelets to the endothelial surface. Functions as a sensor and mechanotransducer of the fluid shear forces to which the endothelium is exposed; thus the glycocalyx mediates shear-stress-dependent nitric oxide production. Retains protective enzymes (eg. superoxide dismutase). Retains anticoagulation factors, eg: Tissue factor inhibitor Protein C Antithrombin any atherosclerotic processes inflammation - TNF alpha
hypervolaemia - ANP ischaemic/reperfusion sepsis trauma surgery ↑ capillary permeabiity hypercoagulability; platelet aggregation inflammation
#peripheral-vascular-physiology #cardio
https://derangedphysiology.com/main/required-reading/sepsis-and-infections/Chapter-131/significance-endothelial-glycocalyx

item.title: Va-Q mismatch
item.description:
e.g. PE = physiologic dead space = Va/Q --> infinity anatomical dead space = bits of the respiratory tract that don't participate in gas exchange e.g. nose, pharynx... → measured using Fowler method alveolar dead space alveoli not participating in gas exchange... because of poor perfusion in a healthy adult, this should be negligible anatomic + alveolar = physiologic dead space → measured using Bohr equation 150ml in the "frictionless cow"/average adult male Calculation of dead space can be done by Fowler's method = physiologic shunt = Va/Q --> 0#respiratory #resp-physiology

item.title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
item.description:
acute diffuse, inflammatory lung injury increased pulmonary vascular permeability, increased lung weight, and loss of aerated lung tissue hypoxemia and bilateral radiographic opacities, associated with increased venous admixture, increased physiological dead space and decreased lung compliance. acute onset (within 1/52) not exclusively or primarily attributable to cardiogenic pulmonary edema/fluid overload radiologic evidence: Bilateral opacities on chest radiography and computed tomography or bilateral B lines and/or consolidations on ultrasound not fully explained by effusions, atelectasis, or nodules/masses P/F ratio Injury Exudative – alveolar capillary membrane disruption with inflammatory cell infiltrate and high protein exudate to form hyaline membranes → damage to alveolar-capillary barrier => pulmonary oedema Proliferative – proliferation of abnormal Type II alveoli cells and inflammatory cells Fibrotic – infiltration with fibroblasts which replace alveoli and alveolar ducts with fibrosis Resolution – slow and incomplete repair and restoration of architecture Lung protective ventilation
Non-ventilatory strategies for ARDS
#icu #respiratory #ventilation

item.title: NNT absolute risk reduction
item.description:
The number of patients you need to treat to prevent one additional bad outcome = 1/ARR where ARR = CER (Control Event Rate) – EER (Experimental Event Rate). The number of patients who, if they received the experimental treatment, would lead to one additional person being harmed compared with patients who receive the control treatment; = 1/ARI (absolute risk increase) may also be called attributable risk= control event rate - experimental event rate#evidence-based-medicine

item.title: Cardiac contractility
item.description:
Catecholamines Ca influx via phosphorylation of Ca channels Ischaemia when intracellular Ca can't release more Ca from sarcolemma Hypocalcaemia (huh) Temperature ↓ myocardial sensitivity to calcium, and ↓ activity of actin-activated myosin ATPase Myocyte contraction is the consequence of significant calcium influx into the myocytes Relaxation is mainly due to this calcium being ejected back out of the cell, or re-sequestered into the sarcolemma This expulsion of calcium is a chemical process with a finite reaction time Ergo, with increased heart rate, the time left for the removal of calcium is decreased Ergo, the residual calcium will increase the contractility of the myocytes wherever a high heart rate is sustained. Not unique to cardiac myocytes #physiology #cardiac-physiology

Cardiac effects of calcium

item.title: blood-brain barrier
item.description:
diffusion barrier impedes passage of most compounds from blood to brain non-fenestrated endothelial cells i.e. continuous lipid bilayer with tight junctions in between basal lamina (basement membrane) pericytes astrocyte foot processes - ensheaths capillaries perivascular potential space physical barrier - because of tight junctions transport barrier - active transport mechanisms are the gatekeepers metabolic barrier - ?? easy diffusion across a lipid bilayer → small high lipid solubility low volume of distribution For specifically hydrophilic drugs: A high concentration in the blood stream, to rely on the concentration gradient to force the drug through the paracellular route (eg. ethanol) Low protein binding, so that a large free fraction is available molecular similarity with another actively transported substance e.g. Lithium (pretends it's sodium)
https://derangedphysiology.com/main/cicm-primary-exam/nervous-system/Chapter-111/blood-brain-barrier
Disruption can lead to cerebral oedema.

item.title: Haemoglobin
item.description:
HbA = a2 b2 = the population average HbA2 = a2 delta 2 HbF = a2 gamma 2 basically has an openable hydrophobic pocket Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the sixth codon of beta-globin that leads to the replacement of a glutamate residue with a valine residue (Robbins) essentially good transporter for small molecules due to shape and binding sites iron ion in haem can go between 2+ and 3+ → participate in redox reactions!
Oxygen transport (affinity described by the oxygen dissociation curve) CO2 transport NO scavenging (NO binds to ferric ion) → contributes to regional autoregulation! Quoted clinical examples:
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, and the pulmonary hypertension seen with polycythaemia (​​​​​Deem, 2004).
Sickle cell vasoconstrictive crisis (Mack & Kato, 2004) Buffering? (histidine groups)
(via haem oxygenase) bilverdin → (biliverdin reductase) bilirubin (See Bilirubin metabolism) 🏠 hepatocytes
#haematology
https://derangedphysiology.com/main/cicm-primary-exam/haematological-system/Chapter-011/structure-and-function-haemoglobin#:~:text=the%20haemoglobin%20molecule.-,Haem,-Each%20haemoglobin%20monomer

item.title: diuretics rang dale
Respiratory equations
item.description: Flow = ∆P/RR = (8VL)/ πr4Ohm's law V = RI , or R = V/I→ adapted to R = ∆P/Q Peripheral vascular resistance = resistance (pressure drop) generated in blood flowing through the whole arterial circulation. the total pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the component gases. For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure (P) and volume (V) are inversely proportional, such that P ×V = k, where k is a constant. The volume occupied by a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V/T = k). Third gas law (Gay-Lussac's Law): The pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (P/T = k). Avogadro's Law: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules (6.023 × 1023, Avogadro’s number). Universal (Ideal) Gas Law: The state of a fixed mass of gas is determined by its pressure, volume and temperature(PV = nRT) Henry's Law The amount of a given gas dissolved in a given liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas in contact with the liquid: => higher pressure increases solubility P = Hv × M Where P is pressure M is the molar concentration of gas Hv is Henry's Proportionality Constant #respiratory #physiology

Oculosympathetic pathway
item.description:
A 3 body problem 3 neuron pathway START in the posterior hypothalamus GOES TO intermediolateral gray column of the spinal cord SYNAPSES at the ciliospinal center of Budge at spinal levels C8 to T2. START in the intermediolateral grey column leaves with ventral spinal roots joins the paravertebral cervical sympathetic chain SYNAPSES at superior cervical ganglion START in superior cervical ganglion enters cranium along internal carotid artery
JOINS the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) within the cavernous sinus SYNAPSES at ciliary muscle and pupillary dilator muscle via the nasociliary nerve and the long ciliary nerves

Cardiac effects of calcium
item.description: Calcium determines contractility Calcium entry into cardiac myocytes triggers a calcium-dependent release of calcium from the sarcolemma Calcium binds to troponin resulting in sliding of the thick and thin filaments Force of contraction depends on the amount of calcium bound to troponin Therefore, the major factor that regulates the force of contraction is the level of intracellular calcium #cardiac-physiology

item.title: Hypernatraemia
item.description:
Usually due to ↓ free water in ICU context Can cause delirium (thirst!!) The alert but not thirsty hypernatraemia patient has a hypothalamic problem Na/K administration usually from fluids and meds that we're giving not enough free water ↑ GI water loss - vomiting, NG aspirate, diarrhoea incl. osmotic laxatives renal water loss due to diabetes insipidus diuresis loop diuretics SGLT-2 inhibitors polyuric phase of AKI recovery (when urea gets cleared, it takes water with it)
Hyperreflexia, myoclonic jerks, nystagmus. (36578134) Weakness Urine Osm (physiologically expect to be high → inappropriately low or normal Osm suggest DI) What is the free water deficit?
#endocrine
